quotes.text: Co-pilot respects permissions. If someone can access a file, co-pilot may use that file as context for that person. So your permission model becomes your AI access model.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Explains in one line why permission cleanup is a prerequisite for Copilot.

quotes.text: Copilot can reduce effort within a task, but reduced effort does not automatically create financial return.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters

quotes.text: A deployment plan, without a stop condition, is usually a spending plan wearing a project badge.

quotes.text: Don't connect the system because someone says all our data should be available to AI. That is not an architecture principle. It is a future incident report waiting for a date.

quotes.why: Warns against connecting data sources without ownership and purpose.

quotes.text: Usage data tells you whether people open the tool. It does not tell you whether the tool improves the work.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Clarifies why usage reports are not proof of Copilot value.

takeaways: Treat Microsoft 365 Copilot as a phased business decision built around measurable scenarios, not as a tenant-wide license event.
Existing permissions and information architecture define Copilot's risk boundary, so fix identity, review oversharing and set durable label and DLP controls before broad access.
Prove value with baselines, outcome measures and clear expand, fix or stop decisions, then scale through repeatable scenario clusters with governance and role-based adoption.
hook: Licenses are bought and the pilot group is waiting, but can anyone say what Copilot will expose through today's permissions? This episode gives CIOs, security leaders and Microsoft 365 teams a consultant's playbook for deploying Microsoft 365 Copilot across an enterprise, from readiness and permission cleanup to governance, pilots, ROI and scaling.
